clinicalPearls: Pain is centred over the lateral epicondyle and the origin of the common wrist extensors, often radiating down the back of the forearm
Symptoms are provoked by gripping, lifting with the palm down, and resisted wrist or middle-finger extension
Despite the older term epicondylitis, the underlying process is a degenerative tendinopathy rather than acute inflammation
It most commonly affects the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin and peaks in middle age, frequently in people doing repetitive forearm work rather than tennis players
Diagnosis is clinical; local tenderness just distal to the epicondyle with pain on resisted extension is characteristic
First-line management is activity modification, load reduction, and a progressive eccentric or graded strengthening programme, which addresses the underlying tendon problem
Counterforce bracing and attention to technique and equipment can offload the tendon during aggravating activities
Corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but is associated with poorer long-term outcomes and higher recurrence than exercise-based rehabilitation
Most cases are self-limiting over months to a couple of years, and surgery is reserved for the small minority with refractory symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Tennis elbow is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle, most often involving extensor carpi radialis brevis. Repetitive gripping and wrist extension produce microtears and a failed healing response, with angiofibroblastic (mucoid) degeneration, disorganised collagen, and neovascularisation rather than true inflammatory change. The weakened tendon becomes painful and mechanically vulnerable to further load.
additionalDifferentials: Radial tunnel syndrome (posterior interosseous nerve entrapment)
Cervical radiculopathy referring pain to the lateral forearm
Posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow
Referred pain from the shoulder or myofascial trigger points
additionalInvestigations: Usually a clinical diagnosis requiring no imaging
Ultrasound can confirm tendon thickening, hypoechoic change, or tears and guide injection when the diagnosis is unclear
MRI in atypical or refractory cases to characterise the tendon and exclude intra-articular pathology
Plain radiographs if bony pathology or calcification is suspected
Nerve conduction studies if radial tunnel syndrome or radiculopathy is considered
redFlags: Night pain, systemic symptoms, or a mass suggesting infection or tumour rather than tendinopathy
Neurological symptoms pointing to nerve entrapment or cervical radiculopathy
History of significant trauma raising the possibility of instability or fracture
Failure to improve despite appropriate rehabilitation, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The natural history is generally favourable, with most patients recovering within a year regardless of specific treatment, though symptoms can persist or recur; structured loading rehabilitation improves long-term outcomes compared with steroid injection.
pitfalls: Assuming an inflammatory process and relying on rest and anti-inflammatories rather than progressive loading
Repeated corticosteroid injections, which can worsen the tendon and long-term prognosis
Overlooking radial tunnel syndrome or cervical radiculopathy in atypical or persistent cases
Neglecting kinetic-chain, technique, and workplace factors that perpetuate overload
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Base treatment on activity modification and load reduction, avoiding the repetitive gripping and wrist extension that drive the tendinopathy
Prescribe a progressive eccentric or graded resistance strengthening programme for the wrist extensors as the definitive rehabilitation, addressing the failed tendon healing
Provide short-term analgesia with topical or oral NSAIDs for pain control
Consider a counterforce forearm brace to offload the common extensor origin during aggravating activity
Reassure the patient about the generally favourable, self-limiting natural history over months to a year
Reserve corticosteroid injection for short-term relief only, counselling that it can worsen long-term outcome compared with loading rehabilitation
Refer for physiotherapy, and consider extracorporeal shockwave therapy or surgical debridement and release in refractory, prolonged cases
